title: Thoth: Lord of Divine Words
summary: A month with Djehuty, the ibis and the baboon, scribe of the gods, reckoner of the moon and the years. Study his myths, his cult and the much later Hermes Trismegistus, keep ten nights at the writing desk, and decide whether to dedicate.
welcome:
This journey spends about a lunar month with Thoth, the Egyptian god of writing, knowledge, reckoning and the moon. He suits people who study, write, keep records, teach, translate or measure, and anyone who wants to think more clearly and speak more truly.

You will learn who he was in Egypt, his myths, how the ibis and the baboon came to be his, how scribes and ordinary people honoured him, and how he became, much later, the Hermes Trismegistus of Western esotericism. For ten nights you will work at your desk in his presence. At the end you may dedicate yourself, or not.

This is a self-dedication. It is not an initiation into Kemetic Orthodoxy, a Hermetic order or any other group, and it does not replace one. Thoth would want you to check everything you read here, including this.
about: Thoth (Egyptian Djehuty) was the god of writing and of everything writing makes possible: knowledge, law, calculation, record-keeping, magic spells, medicine and the calendar. He was also a moon god, who measured time by its phases. He appears as a man with the head of an ibis, holding a scribe's palette and reed pen, or as a baboon, often crowned with the crescent and full moon. His great city was Khemenu, "Eight-town", the Greeks' Hermopolis, in Middle Egypt (modern el-Ashmunein). In myth he is the gods' scribe, messenger and judge: he records the verdict when the hearts of the dead are weighed, heals the Eye of Horus, settles the quarrel between Horus and Set, and gives Isis spells to protect her son. Greeks identified him with Hermes, and late antiquity built the figure of Hermes Trismegistus on his name, the source of the Hermetic tradition. Today he is honoured in Kemetic religion, both by reconstructionists and in Kemetic Orthodoxy, and he is loved by many students and writers of every path.
notes: Hermes Trismegistus, the Corpus Hermeticum, the Emerald Tablet and the "Thoth" tarot are later Greek, Arabic, European and modern creations that grew from his name. They are worth studying, but they are not Egyptian worship of Djehuty.
The "Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean" (1930s) is a modern work by the American writer Doreal. It has no ancient source.

The popular claim that every Egyptian scribe poured a drop of water for Thoth before writing is repeated in many books, but no ancient text or image showing it has been traced. Scribes certainly honoured Thoth. Treat the libation as a modern custom, and a good one.
Millions of ibises and many baboons were mummified as offerings to Thoth. Do not buy animal mummies or other antiquities; reproductions and pictures are better offerings.
Kemetic religion is a living practice with its own communities and customs. Ask before joining their spaces.
Safety: never put ink, pigments or stones in drinks; keep incense smoke away from pet birds.

stages.title: Opening the Palette
stages.intro: Begin by learning who Thoth is and making a shrine where you write or study. The threshold ends with a short introduction rite: you greet him and write your first words in his presence.

lessons.title: Djehuty of Khemenu
lessons.summary: His name, his two animals, his city, his moon and his titles.

sections.heading: Ibis and baboon
sections.body:
Thoth had two animals, and Egyptians never felt the need to choose between them. The first is the sacred ibis, a white wading bird with a black head and a long down-curved beak, which probes the mud as a scribe's pen moves across papyrus. The ibis-headed man with palette and pen is his most familiar form. The sacred ibis no longer lives wild in Egypt, but it survives further south in Africa.

The second is the hamadryas baboon, often shown squatting with its hands on its knees, crowned with a crescent and a full moon. Baboons are noisy at sunrise, and Egyptians saw them as adoring the sun, so baboons also appear in solar scenes. A small New Kingdom statuette in the Louvre shows the scribe Nebmertef at work, cross-legged, with a baboon of Thoth perched above him: the god watching over the work.

sections.heading: His name and city
sections.body:
His Egyptian name, Djehuty, probably means "he of Djehut", an old place-name, though this is not certain. "Thoth" is the Greek form. His great city was Khemenu, "Eight-town", named for the Ogdoad, four pairs of primeval gods who in Hermopolitan teaching existed before creation: Nun and Naunet (the waters), Heh and Hauhet (infinity), Kek and Kauket (darkness), Amun and Amaunet (hiddenness). Thoth was lord of this place of beginnings.

The Greeks called the city Hermopolis, "city of Hermes", because they identified Thoth with their own messenger god. Little stands there today, but two colossal quartzite baboons set up by King Amenhotep III, over four metres tall, still sit at el-Ashmunein.

sections.heading: The moon and the reckoning
sections.body:
Thoth was a moon god, and for Egyptians the moon was a clock. The lunar month governed temple festivals, and the moon's waxing and waning was the measure of time itself. Thoth was "the one who reckons the years", who with the goddess Seshat wrote the king's years on the leaves of a sacred tree. He also measured the earth, the Nile flood and the fields.

The first month of the Egyptian year bore his name in its Greek form, Thoth, and it still does in the Coptic calendar used by the Coptic Church and Egyptian farmers, where the month Thout begins around 11 September.

sections.heading: His titles and companions
sections.body:
He was Neb Medu Netjer, "Lord of Divine Words": hieroglyphs themselves were called medu netjer, "god's words", and Thoth had given them. He was the Lord of Ma'at, because accurate records and true speech keep the world in order. He was the heart and tongue of Ra, the thinking and the speaking of the creator. Late Egyptian texts call him "twice great" and even "three times great", the root of the Greek Trismegistos.

His companion in writing was Seshat, "she who writes", goddess of measuring and of libraries, who helped kings stretch the cord to lay out new temples. At Hermopolis his consort was Nehmetawy. Some texts pair him with Ma'at herself.

knowAndDont.known: His ibis and baboon forms, his cult at Hermopolis, his role as scribe and lunar reckoner, the Ogdoad, the Amenhotep III baboons and the Nebmertef statuette are all securely attested.
knowAndDont.unknown: The meaning of the name Djehuty is uncertain, and so is why he came to have two quite different animals. Hermopolis itself is poorly preserved, so much of its theology is known only from texts elsewhere.

lessons.inPractice: Choose a name to use (Djehuty or Thoth) and an image: an ibis, an ibis-headed scribe, or a baboon with the moon. Many devotees keep their shrine on or beside their desk. Learn the current moon phase, since you will be keeping time by it.
reflect: What do you write, study or keep records of in your life now? What would you like to?
Which of his animals speaks to you, the patient ibis or the dawn-greeting baboon?
further: Richard H. Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003), entry on Thoth
Patrick Boylan, Thoth, the Hermes of Egypt (1922)

practices.title: Set up a shrine at your desk
practices.instructions:
Clear a small corner of your desk or a shelf beside it. Clean it with water that has a pinch of natron, washing soda or salt in it.

Lay a clean white or blue cloth. Place his image at the back. In front, set a small water cup, a dish for bread or a date, an incense burner on a heatproof tile, and a white or silver candle. Add a good pen, a small notebook kept only for him, and a crescent-moon symbol. Lapis lazuli or fluorite suit him.

Keep the shrine tidy. Of all the gods, Thoth is the one whose shrine should not disappear under unopened post and old coffee cups.
practices.prompt: What did you set on his shrine, and what did you clear away to make room?

rite.title: Introduction to Thoth
rite.summary: A short first visit: purify, greet him, offer water, bread and incense, and write your first words in his notebook.

ingredients.name: A small cup of fresh water
Natron, washing soda or salt dissolved in a cup of water
A piece of bread or a few dates
Frankincense, myrrh or cedar incense and a burner
A good pen and a new notebook

rite.preparation: Wash your hands and face and rinse your mouth with the natron or salt water, spitting it out. Clear your desk. Put away your phone.

steps.title: Light and purify
steps.instructions: Light the candle and the incense. Touch the natron water to your lips and pass your hands through the smoke.
steps.spoken: I am pure. My hands are clean and my mouth is clean. I come before the lord of divine words.

steps.title: Greet him
steps.instructions: Raise both hands, palms toward his image, at face height.
steps.spoken: Homage to you, Djehuty, lord of Khemenu, lord of divine words, reckoner of the moon and the years. I greet you.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Lift the water, then the bread, toward him and set them down. Hold the incense up for a moment.
steps.spoken: An offering for Djehuty: cool water, bread and sweet smoke. May they please you.

steps.title: Write your first words
steps.instructions: Open the new notebook. Write the date, your name, and in a few honest sentences why you have come to him and what you hope to learn. Write slowly and as neatly as you can. If you wish, touch a drop of the offering water to the corner of the page first.

steps.title: Read it to him
steps.instructions: Read what you wrote aloud, then sit quietly for a minute.
steps.spoken: This is my word, written before you. Let it be true.

steps.title: Close
steps.instructions: Thank him and snuff the candle. Close the notebook and leave it on his shrine.
steps.spoken: Go in peace, Djehuty. I will come again to learn.

rite.closing: Eat the bread or dates later; this is the reversion of offerings. Pour the water on a plant. Keep the notebook only for your work with him.
rite.safety: Keep candle and incense on a heatproof tile, well away from paper and books, in a ventilated room, and never leave them unattended. Keep smoke away from pet birds. Do not swallow the natron water.

stages.title: The Scribe of the Gods
stages.intro: Three lessons: his myths; how Egypt honoured him, from great animal cemeteries to a scribe’s prayer; and the later Hermes Trismegistus. Keep a few minutes at his shrine before you study each day.

lessons.title: Healer, Judge and Keeper of Time
lessons.summary: The main myths of Thoth, and a famous Greek story about him.

sections.heading: The Eye of Horus and the trial
sections.body:
In the long struggle between Horus and Set over the throne of Osiris, Set tore out Horus's eye. Thoth found it, healed it and gave it back. The healed eye, the wedjat, became one of the most common amulets in Egypt, a sign of wholeness and protection. In some versions Thoth also heals the injuries Set suffered, because he restores balance, not just one side.

In the New Kingdom tale called the Contendings of Horus and Set, the gods argue for eighty years in court over who should inherit. Thoth is the clerk and counsellor of the court, writing the letters, advising the judges, and in the end helping to bring a just verdict for Horus. He is calm in a story where almost nobody else is.

sections.heading: At the weighing of the heart
sections.body:
In the Book of the Dead judgement scene, the heart of the dead person is weighed against the feather of Ma'at. Anubis checks the balance; Thoth, ibis-headed, stands with his palette and records the result. Sometimes a baboon of Thoth sits on top of the scale. Budge describes him there as "Thoth, the scribe of the gods, ibis-headed, holding in his hands a reed wherewith to write down the result of the weighing."

Egyptians prayed that Thoth would be their advocate, as he had been for Osiris when Set brought charges against him before the gods. Truthful record-keeping was not dry work to them. It was what made justice possible, in this life and the next.

sections.heading: The five days and the Distant Goddess
sections.body:
Plutarch, writing in Greek around 100 CE, tells a story about how the five extra days at the end of the Egyptian year came to be. The sky goddess had been cursed so that she could not give birth on any day of the year. So Hermes, Plutarch's name for Thoth, played a board game with the Moon. In F. C. Babbitt's translation (1936): "playing at draughts with the moon, he won from her the seventieth part of each of her periods of illumination, and from all the winnings he composed five days". On those days Osiris, Horus, Set, Isis and Nephthys were born. There is no full Egyptian version of this story, so treat it as Plutarch's.

An Egyptian story with deep roots tells how the Eye of Ra, the fierce goddess Tefnut, left Egypt in anger for Nubia. Thoth, in baboon form, went after her and coaxed her home with stories and fables. Its fullest version, the Myth of the Eye of the Sun, is a late demotic text. Thoth is a god who brings things back by talking, not by force.

sections.heading: A Greek warning about writing
sections.body:
Plato tells a story in the Phaedrus, written in Athens in the fourth century BCE, in which Theuth (Thoth) brings his inventions to the king of Egypt, Thamus, and praises letters as a cure for forgetting. The king disagrees. In Benjamin Jowett's translation: "this discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves."

This is a Greek philosopher's story, not an Egyptian myth; even Phaedrus answers that Socrates can easily invent tales of Egypt. But it is a good thing for a devotee of Thoth to sit with. Writing is a tool, and knowing things means more than having them written down.

knowAndDont.known: Thoth’s healing of the Eye of Horus, his role in the Contendings (Papyrus Chester Beatty I) and in the judgement scene (Book of the Dead ch. 125 vignettes) are well attested, as is his link with the baboon and the return of the Distant Goddess.
knowAndDont.unknown: The board game with the Moon is known only from Plutarch. The Myth of the Eye of the Sun survives mainly in late demotic papyri and earlier allusions; how old the full story is, is uncertain. Plato’s tale is Greek invention around an Egyptian name.

lessons.inPractice: Wear or keep a wedjat eye as a sign of restoration. When you face a dispute, try Thoth’s way: write the facts down accurately before you argue. Read the Phaedrus passage and write a page on how you use writing to remember, or to avoid remembering.
reflect: Where in your life is an "eye" that needs restoring, and what would Thoth’s patient care look like there?
Do you agree with Thamus? What does writing give you, and what does it take?
further: Plato, Phaedrus, trans. Benjamin Jowett, Project Gutenberg
Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 2, for the Contendings of Horus and Seth
Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris §12, trans. F. C. Babbitt (Loeb, 1936; public domain, at LacusCurtius)

lessons.title: Ibis Cemeteries and Scribes’ Prayers
lessons.summary: How Thoth was honoured: temples and animal cults, the scribes, his festival, and Egyptian offering customs.

sections.heading: Millions of ibises
sections.body:
In the Late and Ptolemaic periods, from about the seventh century BCE, pilgrims honoured Thoth by paying for a mummified ibis or baboon to be buried in his catacombs. At Tuna el-Gebel, the cemetery of Hermopolis, and at Saqqara near Memphis, underground galleries hold millions of ibis mummies in pots. A genetic study published in 2019 suggested that most were wild birds caught and kept near temples, rather than birds bred in huge farms, as had been thought.

Saqqara also had an oracle and a place of dream incubation for Thoth. A priest there in the second century BCE, Hor of Sebennytos, kept an archive of his own dreams and petitions on potsherds, a rare glimpse of one man's devotion. Pilgrims slept in the temple hoping that Thoth would send a dream to answer their questions.

sections.heading: The scribes’ god
sections.body:
Scribes were Egypt's educated class, perhaps a few per cent of the population, and Thoth was theirs. Their palettes, long slips of wood with wells for black and red ink and a slot for reed pens, sometimes carry invocations to Thoth alongside prayers for offerings. School texts of the New Kingdom, the so-called Late Egyptian Miscellanies, include short prayers in which a scribe begs Thoth to come to him, to make him skilled, to take him to Hermopolis where life is sweet. Statues show officials as scribes beneath a baboon of Thoth.

You will often read that every scribe poured a drop of water from his water pot as a libation to Thoth before starting work. It is a lovely idea and many modern devotees do it. But no one has yet pointed to an ancient text or image that shows it; popular books repeat it without a source. The palette invocations and scribes' prayers are real; the drop of water is best called a modern custom inspired by them.

sections.heading: His festival
sections.body:
Egyptian festival calendars mark a feast of Thoth in the first month of the year, the month that carries his name, around the 19th day. Plutarch adds a detail. In Babbitt's translation: "on the nineteenth day of the first month, when they are holding festival in honour of Hermes, they eat honey and a fig; and as they eat they say, 'A sweet thing is Truth.'" That is a delightful custom to revive, and it comes from a Greek writer describing the Egypt of his own time.

The new moon and full moon were also his. The Egyptian lunar month began on the morning when the old crescent could no longer be seen, and lunar feast days were kept in temples throughout the year.

sections.heading: How to offer
sections.body:
The customs of every Egyptian god apply. Come pure: wash your hands and face, rinse your mouth, wear clean clothes. Use the shape of the temple rite: purify, open, adore, offer, close. Speak the offering formula in your own words, since words were gifts in themselves, and for Thoth that is especially fitting. Afterwards eat or share the food, which is the reversion of offerings, and give the water to a plant.

Fitting gifts for Thoth: water and bread, as the Library entry suggests; honey and figs; frankincense or cedar; fresh ink, good paper or a new pen; a hymn copied by hand; a piece of finished work, honestly done.

knowAndDont.known: The ibis catacombs of Tuna el-Gebel and Saqqara, the 2019 DNA study (Wasef and colleagues), the archive of Hor of Sebennytos, scribes’ palettes with invocations and the Late Egyptian Miscellanies prayers are documented. Plutarch records the honey-and-fig custom.
knowAndDont.unknown: The scribe’s drop-of-water libation is not traceable to a clear ancient source. How far ordinary people, rather than scribes and priests, prayed to Thoth is hard to say. The exact festival day varied between calendars.

lessons.inPractice: Keep the drop of water before you write, if you like, knowing it is a modern custom. On his festival, or on any day of study, eat honey and a fig and say "A sweet thing is Truth". Before you sleep on a hard question, write it down and leave it at his shrine; note any dream in the morning.
reflect: Does it change the custom for you that the scribe’s libation is modern? Why or why not?
What is the most honest work you could offer him this month?
further: J. D. Ray, The Archive of Hor (1976)
Sally Wasef et al., "Mitogenomic diversity in Sacred Ibis mummies sheds light on early Egyptian practices", PLOS ONE (2019)

lessons.title: From Djehuty to Hermes Trismegistus
lessons.summary: How Thoth became the patron of Hermeticism, alchemy and tarot, and how to tell the layers apart.

sections.heading: Thoth becomes Hermes
sections.body:
When Greeks settled in Egypt, they matched Egyptian gods to their own. Thoth, messenger and god of clever words, became Hermes. Late Egyptian titles calling Thoth "great, great" or "thrice great" became the Greek Hermes Trismegistos, "thrice-greatest Hermes". By the Roman period this figure had become a legendary sage, a teacher of philosophy, astrology and magic, sometimes said to be an ancient human king rather than a god.

Greek magical papyri from Roman Egypt invoke Hermes-Thoth in spells, mixing Egyptian, Greek and Jewish elements. This is a real and fascinating religious world. It is also several centuries and a language away from the temples of Hermopolis.

sections.heading: The Hermetic books
sections.body:
The Corpus Hermeticum is a set of Greek philosophical dialogues, written probably in the second and third centuries CE, in which Hermes teaches his son Tat about God, the mind and the soul. They are Greek in thought, though some scholars find Egyptian ideas in them. The Emerald Tablet, with its famous "as above, so below" idea, is first known in Arabic texts of the eighth to tenth centuries.

When the Corpus reached Florence in the 1460s, Marsilio Ficino translated it, and Renaissance thinkers took Hermes for a sage older than Moses. In 1614 the scholar Isaac Casaubon showed from its language that it was written in the Christian era. Hermeticism lived on all the same in alchemy, Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry and the Golden Dawn.

sections.heading: Tarot and the Book of Thoth
sections.body:
In 1781 the French writer Antoine Court de Gébelin claimed that the tarot was an ancient Egyptian book of Thoth's wisdom. Tarot cards were in fact invented in fifteenth-century Italy for a card game, and Egyptian hieroglyphs had not yet been deciphered when he wrote. His idea spread through French occultism and the Golden Dawn, and Aleister Crowley named his deck and book after Thoth (published in 1944, the cards in 1969).

There was an Egyptian Book of Thoth, of a kind. A demotic story about Prince Setne Khaemwas tells of a magical scroll written by Thoth, hidden in nested boxes at the bottom of the river at Koptos, that brings disaster on those who steal it. And scholars have reconstructed a real demotic text now called the Book of Thoth, a dialogue between a student and Thoth about scribal knowledge.

sections.heading: Telling the layers apart
sections.body:
None of this makes Hermeticism or tarot worthless; for many people they are a real path, and Thoth as Hermes is honoured sincerely. The problem is only with claims that these things are ancient Egyptian when they are not. The worst case is the "Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean", published in the 1930s by an American occultist who called himself Doreal. It is a modern composition with no ancient source at all.

A simple test, and a Thoth-like one: ask where a text comes from, when it was written, and in what language. If nobody can tell you, be careful.

knowAndDont.known: The Greek identification of Thoth with Hermes, the Greek Magical Papyri, the dating of the Corpus Hermeticum (Casaubon, 1614), the Arabic origin of the Emerald Tablet, the Italian origin of tarot and Court de Gébelin’s 1781 claim are well established.
knowAndDont.unknown: How much genuine Egyptian thought lies behind the Hermetic books is still debated; scholars such as Garth Fowden argue for real Egyptian roots. The exact path by which the epithet "thrice great" moved from Egyptian into Greek is not fully clear.

lessons.inPractice: Decide whether you are honouring Djehuty of Egypt, Hermes Trismegistus of the Hermetic tradition, or both, and say which at his shrine. If you read tarot or Hermetic texts in his name, enjoy them as what they are. Apply the source test to anything that claims to be "the secret teaching of Thoth".
reflect: Which Thoth are you drawn to: the Egyptian god, the Hermetic sage, or the patron of tarot?
What would it mean to make checking your sources an act of devotion?
further: Brian P. Copenhaver, Hermetica (1992), a translation of the Corpus Hermeticum
Richard Jasnow and Karl-Theodor Zauzich, The Ancient Egyptian Book of Thoth (2005)
Michael Dummett, The Game of Tarot (1980)

practices.title: Water before study
practices.instructions: Before each study or writing session, wash your hands, give fresh water at his shrine, raise your hands and say a line of greeting. If you like, touch a drop of water to your pen or page. Afterwards, write one line in his notebook about what you did.
practices.prompt: One line: what did you learn or write today?

stages.title: Ten Nights at the Desk
stages.intro: For ten nights, one Egyptian "week", you will work in Thoth’s presence: an offering, a passage copied by hand, and honest work. If you can, begin on the day after the new moon, when the Egyptian lunar month began. First read the lesson on honouring him today.

lessons.title: Thoth Today: Practice, Days and Care
lessons.summary: Modern communities, a working shrine, his offerings and days, and the sensitive points.

sections.heading: Who honours him now
sections.body:
Thoth is much loved in Kemetic religion, the modern revival of Egyptian religion. Reconstructionists honour him with offerings modelled on the temple rite and with careful study, which many count as worship in itself. Kemetic Orthodoxy, an organised temple founded in 1988 by Tamara Siuda and based in Illinois, includes him in its calendar and devotions. Independent Kemetics often keep a Thoth shrine on their desk.

Beyond Kemetic religion, Thoth is honoured by Hermeticists and ceremonial magicians as Hermes Trismegistus, by tarot readers, and by eclectic Pagans and witches who see him as a god of magic and learning. Students and writers of many faiths simply light a candle to him before exams. Each of these is its own practice; none needs to pretend to be another.

sections.heading: A shrine that works
sections.body:
A Thoth shrine is a working shrine. Keep it where you study or write, clean and orderly. Keep a notebook for him alone, and write in it after each session: what you did, what you learned, what you got wrong. Over a year it becomes a record he would approve of.

Give water before work. Give bread, dates, figs and honey as food offerings, and eat them afterwards. Burn frankincense or cedar while you study, if your space allows it. Copy hymns and prayers by hand. Dedicate a finished piece of work to him: an essay, a translation, a carefully kept set of accounts.

sections.heading: His days
sections.body:
His great festival falls in the first month of the Egyptian year, around the 19th; Plutarch's honey, fig and "A sweet thing is Truth" belong here. Modern Kemetics place the first month variously. Calendars beginning with the rising of Sirius put it in late summer; the Coptic calendar's month Thout begins around 11 September, putting the 19th around the end of that month.

The new and full moons are his too, and many devotees keep a short lunar offering each month. In Western astrology, Wednesday is the day of Mercury, and some people honour Thoth then; that comes through the Greek Hermes and Roman Mercury, not from Egypt, and it is fine if you know it.

sections.heading: Sensitive points
sections.body:
Honesty is the heart of his worship. Copying someone else's work and calling it your own, faking results, or presenting modern ideas as ancient, all sit badly with a god whose job is the true record. That includes the material you read about him; prefer sources that show their evidence.

Animal ethics come up too: millions of ibises died for his cult. Do not buy animal mummies or other antiquities, and if you want to honour his animals, support the conservation of ibises and baboons where they still live.

And remember that Kemet's heritage belongs first to Egypt and to Africa. Learn from Egyptian and African scholars as well as European ones, and treat living Kemetic communities as people with their own customs.

knowAndDont.known: Kemetic Orthodoxy and other Kemetic communities are documented modern movements. The first-month festival, lunar feasts and the Coptic month Thout are attested. The Wednesday link runs through Greek and Roman planetary weeks.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no single modern Kemetic calendar, and ancient festival dates drifted against the seasons because the civil year had no leap day. Many popular associations for Thoth (particular crystals, colours, Wednesdays) are modern.

lessons.inPractice: Keep his notebook going after this journey. Mark his festival and the new and full moons in your calendar. Choose one act of honesty as your standing offering: citing sources, correcting a mistake, keeping true accounts.
reflect: What is the truest record you keep, and what is the least?
How will you keep his days without letting them become one more deadline?
further: Richard J. Reidy, Eternal Egypt: Ancient Rituals for the Modern World (2010)

practices.title: Ten nights at Thoth’s desk
practices.instructions:
Each evening: wash, clear your desk, light the candle and incense, raise your hands to Thoth and greet him. Offer water and a small food offering (bread, a date, a fig with honey). Copy the night's passage or theme into his notebook by hand, slowly and neatly. Then work for at least twenty minutes on something you are studying or writing. Finish by writing one honest line about the session. Snuff the candle.

Night 1: copy a short hymn or prayer to him. Night 2: the ibis; write about patience. Night 3: the baboon at sunrise. Night 4: the Eye of Horus restored. Night 5: the trial of Horus and Set. Night 6: the weighing of the heart. Night 7: the five days won from the Moon. Night 8: the Distant Goddess brought home by stories. Night 9: Thamus's warning about writing. Night 10: "A sweet thing is Truth": eat honey and a fig, and write what is true for you now.

Keep paper well away from the flame, or use a battery candle.
practices.prompt: What did you copy, what did you work on, and what was the one honest line?

stages.title: Checking the Record
stages.intro: Take a few days with only the water before study. Read his notebook from the first page. Dedication is one good outcome; so is pausing, stopping, or finding that another god is calling you.

practices.title: Read the notebook back
practices.instructions: Read his notebook and your journal from the beginning, as a scribe checking a record. Note what is true, what you exaggerated, and what you left out. Then answer the questions below.
practices.prompt: What does the record actually show about this month?

questions: Are you drawn to Thoth himself, or mainly to the discipline of study he helps you keep? Both are worth knowing.
Which Thoth is yours: Djehuty of Egypt, Hermes Trismegistus, or both? Can you say so honestly?
Can you keep a small working practice (water before study, his notebook, his days) through a busy year?
Would a Kemetic community, or a Hermetic order with its own initiations, serve what you are looking for better than a self-dedication?
If you decide to wait or stop, can you write a last honest page, thank him, and close the shrine? That is a good ending too.

stages.title: The Dedication
stages.intro: If you choose to go on, this is your self-dedication to Thoth, a promise you write and speak yourself. It is not an initiation into any Kemetic, Hermetic or other group and does not replace one. His festival, a new or full moon, or the night you finish an important piece of work are all fitting.

rite.title: Self-Dedication to Thoth
rite.summary: A full rite in the Egyptian shape: purification, opening, adoration, offering, the vow written and read aloud, honey and fig for Truth, reversion and closing.

ingredients.name: Natron, washing soda or salt in a cup of water
Bread, a fig and a little honey
Frankincense or cedar and an incense burner
Good paper, and a pen or ink with a reed or dip pen
A wedjat eye or lapis lazuli

rite.preparation:
During the day, draft your vow: what you will do (water before study, his notebook, his festival, honest work), for how long (a year and a day is common), and what you hope for. Keep it short and keepable. You will copy it out fair during the rite.

Wash, rinse your mouth with natron or salt water, and dress in clean clothes. Clear and clean your desk. Set out everything, with paper and pen ready.

steps.title: Purify
steps.instructions: Light the candle and incense, well away from the paper. Wash your hands in the natron water, touch it to your lips, and pass your hands through the smoke.
steps.spoken: I am pure, I am pure. My hands are clean for the pen, my mouth is clean for the word. I come before the lord of divine words.

steps.title: Open and adore
steps.instructions: Uncover his image if it is covered. Raise both hands, palms toward him, and speak the praise.
steps.spoken: Homage to you, Djehuty, lord of Khemenu, lord of divine words, heart and tongue of Ra, reckoner of the moon and the years, who wrote the verdict true and healed the Eye. I praise you.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Lift the water and the bread toward him and set them down. Say the spoken offering.
steps.spoken: An offering for Djehuty: cool water and bread, sweet smoke, every good and pure thing on which a god lives. May it please you.

steps.title: Write the vow
steps.instructions: Touch a drop of the offering water to the corner of the paper. Copy your vow out fair, slowly and as neatly as you can, and date and sign it.

steps.title: Read the vow
steps.instructions: Read it aloud to him, clearly.
steps.spoken: This is my word, written and spoken before you. Record it, Djehuty, and let me keep it true.

steps.title: A sweet thing is Truth
steps.instructions: Dip the fig in honey and eat it, as Plutarch says Egyptians did at his festival, saying the words.

steps.title: Sit with him
steps.instructions: Sit quietly. If words come, write them in his notebook.

steps.title: Reversion and closing
steps.instructions: Thank him. Eat a piece of the bread. Fold the vow and place it in his notebook. Snuff the candle.
steps.spoken: What you have received, I share. Go in peace, Djehuty. I am yours, and I will come again to learn.

rite.closing: Pour the water on a plant. Keep the vow in his notebook and reread it at each new moon. Record the rite in your journal.
rite.safety: Keep candle and incense on a heatproof tile well away from paper, books and ink, in a ventilated room, and never leave them unattended. Keep smoke away from pet birds. Honey is not safe for babies under one year.

stages.title: The Daily Record
stages.intro: After the dedication, the practice is the work itself, done well and offered: water before study, his notebook, his festival and the moons, and a yearly renewal.

practices.title: Water before work
practices.instructions: Before each study or writing session, give fresh water, raise your hands, and say a line of greeting. After it, one honest line in his notebook.

practices.title: New and full moon offering
practices.instructions: At each new moon (or the day after, when the Egyptian month began) and each full moon, give bread and incense, reread your vow, and copy a short passage into his notebook.
practices.prompt: What have you learned since the last moon?

practices.title: His festival
practices.instructions: Keep his festival around the 19th of the first Egyptian month, using the calendar you have chosen (around the end of September by the Coptic reckoning). Give a full offering, eat honey and a fig and say "A sweet thing is Truth", copy a hymn, and dedicate a finished piece of work. Wep Ronpet, the new year, and the epagomenal days before it are good times to review the year's record.
practices.prompt: What did you offer him this year, and what is true for you now?

practices.title: Yearly rededication
practices.instructions: On the anniversary of your dedication or at his festival, read the whole year of his notebook, write a new vow, and repeat the dedication rite. Change the promise honestly. If you are ending the dedication, write a last page of thanks, give a final offering and close the shrine with care.
practices.prompt: What does a year of the record show?
